title: Paul on Trial Before Felix
overview: Jerusalem's temple leaders bring charges against Paul before the Roman governor Felix, Paul answers them point by point, and Felix stalls the case for two years.

parts.label: The case against Paul (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: The high priest brought a hired advocate, Tertullus, who opened by praising Felix, though ancient historians remember Felix as harsh and greedy. He then charged Paul with stirring up unrest across the empire, leading the 'Nazarenes' (followers of Jesus of Nazareth) and trying to defile the temple, all serious matters to Rome (verse 7 is absent from the oldest manuscripts, so many Bibles skip it).

parts.label: No riot, no proof (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: Paul skips the flattery and points to the timeline: he had been in Jerusalem only about twelve days, and he came to worship, not to cause trouble. He challenges his accusers to produce evidence for any of it.

parts.label: Same God, same hope (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Paul admits he follows 'the Way,' an early name for the Jesus movement, but presents it as faithful to Israel's God, Scriptures and hope that the dead will rise and face judgment. This mattered legally, because Rome tolerated Jewish worship and Paul is saying his faith belongs inside it, not outside it.

parts.label: What happened at the temple (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: Paul says he came bringing money for the poor, probably the collection from his churches that he mentions in his letters, and that he had completed the purity rites before entering the temple. He notes that the visitors from Asia (western Turkey) who first accused him are not even present, and that the only 'crime' at the earlier council hearing was speaking about resurrection.

parts.label: Felix puts it off (vv. 22-23)
parts.note: Felix already knew something about the Jesus movement and delayed a verdict until the commander Lysias could come, though the text never says he did. Paul stayed under guard but with some freedom, and friends could bring him what he needed.

parts.label: Uncomfortable talks, long wait (vv. 24-27)
parts.note: Felix and his wife Drusilla, who according to ancient historians had left her first husband to marry him, heard Paul speak about faith in Jesus, doing right, self-control and coming judgment, and it frightened Felix enough to send Paul away. He kept summoning Paul hoping for a bribe, and when his term ended two years later he left Paul in prison to keep the Jerusalem leaders happy.

think: Felix found Paul's words unsettling, yet kept putting off any decision until a 'convenient' time that never seemed to come. What do you think makes it easier to delay a hard question than to face it?
